From national to global: Mapping global center-pivot irrigated cropland with knowledge-guided data augmentation
abstract: Center-pivot irrigated cropland (CPIC) is a large-scale, intensive agricultural irrigation practice with high water-use efficiency. This characteristic enables CPIC to increase crop yields and promote agricultural development, while simultaneously causing groundwater overexploitation and subsequent environmental issues. Mapping the global distribution of CPIC is critical for enhancing water resource management, guiding agricultural policies, and assessing ecological impacts. This study developed a novel methodological framework integrating CPIC prior knowledge into the generation of a global training dataset through designed algorithms, ultimately producing a 2020 global CPIC map (GCMap) based on Landsat imagery. Specifically, we first proposed a shape-prior guided Projection Simulation (PS) to enhance the diversity of national-scale CPIC samples, enabling global CPIC pseudo-label generation through a teacher model. Subsequently, a stratified sampling strategy was implemented to improve sample representativeness across different regions using the pseudo-labels of global CPIC. Furthermore, a dual-temporal correction mechanism was proposed to clean sample labels, ultimately generating high-confidence global training samples. Finally, based on this dataset, a student model was trained using a noise-resistant loss function and deployed on cloud computing platforms to generate the GCMap rapidly. Following Olofsson's design-based stratified sampling and error-matrix framework, we derived statistically rigorous area estimates with explicit 95% confidence intervals and assessed mapping accuracy using the corresponding user's accuracy (UA), producer's accuracy (PA), and overall accuracy (OA) metrics. In comparison with current CPIC products, our GCMap attained a PA of 0.86 ± 0.02, representing a marked reduction in omission errors. Our results show that the global error-adjusted area of CPIC in 2020 was estimated at 18.70 ± 0.42 Mha, representing a 63% increase relative to the previous estimate of 11.5 Mha and revealing substantial underestimation in previous estimates. Geographically, the semi-arid zone has the largest share of CPIC, covering 9.27 ± 0.29 Mha (49.28% of the total), followed by the arid zone (4.69 ± 0.20 Mha, 24.95%) and humid zone (2.99 ± 0.22 Mha, 15.92%). Further analysis indicates that most CPIC is distributed in aquifers with limited underwater recharge. Approximately 15.25 ± 0.87 Mha (82.04%) of CPIC areas are located in regions with recharge rates below 100 mm/year, of which 9.97 ± 0.48 Mha (53.62% of total CPIC) fall within extremely low recharge zones (<20 mm/year). These findings provide an essential foundation for further research on irrigation-groundwater interactions and sustainable policymaking about agricultural development and water usage. Our GCMap inventory is publicly available in an online repository at: https://doi.org/10.12436/GCMap.62.20250711 .

title: GeoPhysAdapter: Scale-matched geophysical adaptation for cross-domain landslide mapping with vision foundation models
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Newly triggered landslides rarely carry immediate annotations, so cross-domain transferability determines the value of landslide mapping for emergency response and regional risk assessment. Vision foundation models have strengthened representational transfer, yet on unseen regions, events, and data sources they still generate high-confidence false alarms. Terrain, material, and rainfall triggering can constrain such errors, but their supports are local, regional, and event-scale, so that resampling onto a 10~m grid misaligns them with the segmentation decision unit and compounds the uncertain geographic context problem (UGCoP). We propose GeoPhysAdapter, which anchors on a frozen vision foundation model, restricts terrain, material, and triggering to dense spatial guidance, regional modulation, and event-timing forcing, and applies bounded adaptation at two decision units, the pixel and the candidate landslide body, reverting exactly to the visual prediction where support is insufficient. On an event-isolated PILD dataset of four public sources, 55 global landslide events, and 7,890 test samples, 70.3% of cross-domain false-positive mass lies in near-pure spurious bodies of median equivalent diameter 207m, matching coarse-prior support rather than the pixel. Pixel-level adaptation removes a net 507,817 erroneous pixels and reduces error by 7.76%, whereas raising the decision unit to the candidate body, under identical samples, anchor, and baseline, increases error reduction to 23.99%, approximately 3.1 times the pixel-level effect, improves IoU by 0.031 (14.2% relative), and corrects 9.92 pixels per pixel harmed. The data and code are publicly available at: https://github.com/Liu-Zhihang/geophysadapter.

A large-scale spatiotemporal NDVI prediction method coupling multivariable constraints and structured modeling
abstract: Accurate prediction of vegetation dynamics is essential for understanding terrestrial ecosystems carbon and water cycles. However, existing Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) prediction methods are limited in their ability to represent spatiotemporal heterogeneity and nonlinear interactions among multiple driving variables, which restrict predictive accuracy and extrapolation performance at large scales. To address these limitations, this study proposed a structured large-scale NDVI spatiotemporal prediction method incorporating multivariable constraints (MCS-LSTP) to characterize vegetation dynamics in complex and heterogeneous environments. MCS-LSTP incorporates multiple key driving variables and enhances the comprehensive representation of complex spatiotemporal dependencies and spatial heterogeneity through homogeneous spatial unit partitioning, unit-level temporal modeling, and continuous surface reconstruction. Results showed that MCS-LSTP model exhibited superior performance in terms of stability and prediction accuracy when compared to AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Random Forest (RF), and Transformer models. The mean Population Stability Index (PSI) reached 0.0572, with 98.7% of prediction units exhibiting PSI values below 0.1, indicating no significant deviation between the observed and simulated NDVI values. The average R2 and RMSE on the test set were 0.8551 and 0.2171, respectively. Furthermore, MCS-LSTP accurately reproduced seasonal NDVI fluctuations and meridional spatial gradients, with particularly high agreement between simulated and reference values during the growing season. This study provides a robust and scalable solution for large-scale NDVI spatiotemporal prediction and offers critical technical support for ecological risk assessment in the Yellow River Basin and other ecologically vulnerable regions.
